Analysis: Both hypotheses integrate exosome biology with miRNA modulation to address EMT-driven chemoresistance, but they differ in focus and practicality. Hypothesis 1 is mechanistically intriguing, proposing that hypoxia-driven selective packaging of miR-155 creates a self-sustaining oncogenic loop. However, its novelty is tempered by unresolved mechanistic details (e.g., the precise sorting machinery) and potential pitfalls related to interfering with endogenous exosomal communication. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 leverages the established anti-EMT role of the miR-200 family by employing engineered exosomes to deliver miR-200 mimics and suppress ZEB1. This approach is translationally appealing, as it offers a targeted and testable therapeutic strategy with clearer in vitro/in vivo endpoints. Although challenges remain in ensuring precise delivery and minimizing off-target effects, the framework is more directly testable and has a more defined safety profile due to its specificity and the ability to optimize exosome engineering. Considering novelty, plausibility, testability, and safety, Hypothesis 2 emerges as the superior proposal.
